query: What makes a situation a system rather than a collection of separate problems?
expected_response:
A situation is a system when its parts are connected in ways that shape one another, so the overall situation cannot be fully understood as a collection of separate problems. The parts may be people, roles, rules, resources, routines, or environmental conditions. What matters is not simply that several problems appear together, but that relationships among them influence what happens: a change in one part can alter the conditions faced by others and change the situation as a whole.

Look for patterns of interaction, dependencies, and feedback. For example, delays in one team may increase pressure on another team, which then rushes work and creates errors that send work back to the first team. Each issue can look like a separate problem when viewed alone, but their interaction forms a reinforcing loop. A system may also contain balancing feedback, bottlenecks, shared incentives, or rules that repeatedly produce the same outcomes even when individuals try to solve the immediate symptoms.

The practical test is whether understanding the connections explains more than a list of isolated issues would. Ask what depends on what, which effects return to influence their causes, and what conditions keep the pattern going. Not every cluster of problems is one system; the relationships must be evidenced rather than assumed. A diagnostic tool such as FSD can be offered afterward if you want to map a specific real-world pattern, but it should not replace the answer to the conceptual question.

expected_doorway.title: Leadership Beyond Control: The Rise of Coherence-Based Governance

assertions: Answers the conceptual question before offering FSD.
Defines systems through evidenced relationships, dependencies, interaction, and feedback.
Does not assume every cluster of problems is a system.
FSD is optional follow-up, never a substitute for the answer.
